title: United States v. McFerrin
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
subject: Cohan Rule Estimation
summary: United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), is a Fifth Circuit R&D credit ruling for U.S. taxpayers claiming credits under I.R.C. § 41. The court held taxpayers may rely on Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 definitions of qualified research and that courts should estimate QREs under Cohan once qualified research is shown, but need not credit after-the-fact reconstructions.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit’s landmark decision in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), stands as one of the most consequential appellate rulings in federal research and development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence. Situated at the intersection of administrative law, federal civil procedure, and tax substantiation doctrine, McFerrin resolved critical disputes regarding the retroactive reliance on Treasury regulations, the rejection of judicially imposed "high innovation" thresholds, and the application of the Cohan estimation rule to qualified research expenses (QREs) under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41. Simultaneously, the litigation exposed severe operational and evidentiary vulnerabilities inherent in retrospective, consultant-driven R&D tax credit studies—specifically regarding uncorroborated oral time reconstructions and the aggressive inclusion of pass-through executive profit-sharing bonuses in the credit base.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Corporate Structure

Arthur R. McFerrin, a prominent chemical engineer, co-founded KMCO, Inc. ("KMCO") in 1975. Operating as a Subchapter S corporation under I.R.C. §§ 1361–1363, KMCO manufactured commodity and specialty chemicals primarily for the petrochemical sector. During the relevant 1999 tax year, McFerrin also owned three other related Subchapter S corporations: KMCO Port Arthur, Inc., doing business as KMTEX ("KMTEX"), South Coast Acquisition, Inc. ("SC Acquisition"), and South Coast Delaware, Inc. ("SC Delaware"). SC Acquisition and SC Delaware served as the sole partners in a separate entity, South Coast Terminals ("SC Terminals").

For the 1999 taxable year, McFerrin and all of the corporate entities originally filed their federal income tax returns in 2000 (Forms 1120S and Form 1040) without claiming any tax credits for increasing research activities under I.R.C. § 41. In May 2003, more than three years after the close of the 1999 tax year, KMCO contracted with a third-party specialty tax consulting firm, alliantgroup, L.P., to conduct a study to determine whether it was eligible for an increasing research tax credit. Relying on the findings of that look-back study, McFerrin and all of the corporations filed amended 1999 tax returns in September 2003. Because Subchapter S corporations and partnerships function as pass-through entities for federal income tax purposes, the claimed research credits flowed directly to the joint individual income tax return (Form 1040X) of Arthur R. McFerrin and his spouse, Dorothy McFerrin, generating an aggregate claimed credit of $472,092.00. The government later contended that part of the refund was attributable to a $6.4 million bonus paid to McFerrin in 1999, which it argued was not a qualified research expense.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Procedural Posture

Less than a month after the September 2003 amended returns were filed, as a result of a clerical error, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued the refund to McFerrin, which, including interest, totaled $601,228.40—comprising the $472,092.00 claimed tax credit plus $129,136.40 in interest—although, according to the government’s complaint, the amended return included no supporting documents to substantiate the claimed credits. Thereafter, the United States Department of Justice, acting on behalf of the IRS, filed a civil action on October 31, 2005, in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas pursuant to I.R.C. § 7405 to recover the erroneous refund plus statutory interest.

This procedural posture altered the conventional allocation of the burden of proof in federal tax litigation. In a standard tax deficiency proceeding before the United States Tax Court or a taxpayer-initiated refund suit under 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1), the Commissioner’s determination enjoys a presumption of correctness, and the taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement to the credit. Conversely, in an action brought by the United States under I.R.C. § 7405 to recover an improperly paid refund, the government acts as the plaintiff and bears the ultimate burden of proof to establish both that an amount was erroneously refunded and the exact quantum of that erroneous refund, as established in Soltermann v. United States, 272 F.2d 387 (9th Cir. 1959), and United States v. Commercial National Bank of Peoria, 874 F.2d 1165 (7th Cir. 1989).

Prior to trial, the district court resolved two threshold procedural issues. First, McFerrin moved to dismiss the government's complaint under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b), arguing that the government’s assertion that he "misrepresented facts" constituted an allegation of fraud or mistake requiring heightened pleading particularity. The district court denied the motion and allowed the case to proceed to trial; on appeal, the Fifth Circuit confirmed that no fraud or mistake had been alleged and that the government had merely alleged a failure to substantiate tax claims with sufficient documentation, which is governed by the liberal notice pleading standard of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2). Second, on summary judgment, the district court held that SC Terminals’ amended return was untimely filed outside the statutory limitations period, ordering McFerrin to repay the portion of the refund attributable to SC Terminals.

The substantiation claims concerning KMCO and KMTEX proceeded to a six-day bench trial. In 2008, the district court (United States v. McFerrin, 102 A.F.T.R.2d 2008-6269 (S.D. Tex. 2008)) entered judgment in favor of the United States, holding that the government had proven by a preponderance of the evidence that the tax credit was not properly supported—finding that, while a few projects "may have involved some research," they were not "qualified research," and that there were no records of the hours worked or supplies used that involved research—and ordering McFerrin to repay the refund with interest.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The substantive dispute in McFerrin centered on the statutory interpretation of I.R.C. § 41, whose predecessor was first enacted in 1981 to incentivize incremental corporate investment in research and development. Under I.R.C. § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer is allowed a credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over a prescribed base amount. Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(1)–(2), in-house QREs consist of wages paid or incurred to an employee for performing "qualified services" (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research) and amounts paid or incurred for "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research.

To constitute "qualified research," an activity must satisfy four separate and independent requirements codified in the conjunctive Four-Part Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1). First, under the Section 174 Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures connected with the research must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenses under I.R.C. § 174, which additionally mandates under I.R.C. § 174(e) that the expenditure be reasonable under the circumstances. Second, under the Technological Information or Discovery Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the taxpayer must intend that the information discovered be useful in the development of a new or improved business component, which I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) defines as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all—defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more—of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, namely a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality under I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)(A).

Crucially, I.R.C. § 41 refers ten separate times to regulations to be promulgated by the Secretary of the Treasury. During the late 1990s and early 2000s, federal courts—including the Tenth Circuit in Tax & Accounting Software Corp. v. United States, 301 F.3d 1254 (10th Cir. 2002), the Seventh Circuit in Eustace v. Commissioner, 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002), and the Tax Court in Norwest Corp. v. Commissioner, 110 T.C. 454 (1998)—interpreted "discovering information" and "process of experimentation" restrictively, requiring taxpayers to discover information new to the world or industry and to conduct formal scientific hypothesis testing.

However, on December 26, 2001, the Treasury Department issued Proposed Regulations (Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4, 66 Fed. Reg. 66362) in which the IRS specifically recognized that its own earlier interpretation of "discovering information" did "not fully address Congress' concerns regarding the importance of research activities to the U.S. economy". These were followed by Final Regulations issued in December 2003 (T.D. 9104, 2004-1 C.B. 406, codified at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4), formally effective for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003. The 2001 Proposed Regulations stated that the IRS generally would not challenge return positions consistent with them and that taxpayers could rely on them until final regulations were published, and the preamble to T.D. 9104 stated that, for taxable years ending before December 31, 2003, the IRS would not challenge return positions consistent with the final regulations.
The Fifth Circuit's Final Holding

On June 9, 2009, the Fifth Circuit vacated the district court’s judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings. Writing for the panel, Circuit Judge Edith Brown Clement established four core holdings that reshaped federal R&D tax credit litigation. First, the appellate court affirmed the district court's denial of McFerrin’s Rule 9(b) motion to dismiss, holding that an erroneous refund suit predicated on a lack of substantiating documentation does not allege fraud or mistake and requires only Rule 8(a)(2) notice pleading. Second, the Fifth Circuit held that the trial court erred on the legal definitions of "qualified research," concluding that the district court erred by applying the superseded judicial definitions from Tax & Accounting Software, Eustace, and Norwest rather than the definitions set forth in the 2001 Proposed Regulations and 2003 Final Regulations (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4). Because the IRS stated in the 2001 Proposed Regulations and in T.D. 9104 that it would not challenge return positions consistent with those regulatory definitions for prior years—and because the government conceded at oral argument that McFerrin could rely on the definitions from the 2003 Regulations in defending the suit—the district court’s factual findings were tainted by an erroneous legal lens and were stripped of appellate deference.

Third, rejecting the government’s harmless-error defense, the Fifth Circuit held that under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540, 544 (2d Cir. 1930), if McFerrin proves on remand that qualified research activities occurred under the proper regulatory standards, the trial court should estimate the allowable QREs associated with those activities—evaluating employee testimony and institutional knowledge—even if the taxpayer lacks exact contemporaneous time-tracking records. Fourth, the Fifth Circuit declined to rule as a matter of law on the government's demand to claw back the refund portion tied to McFerrin’s $6.4 million 1999 bonus, instructing the district court on remand to determine factually under I.R.C. §§ 41(b) and 174(e) what portion, if any, constituted reasonable compensation for qualified services actually performed by McFerrin.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While McFerrin yielded a procedural appellate victory for the taxpayer by vacating the trial court's overly restrictive legal standard, a granular dissection of the record reveals acute operational, technical, and evidentiary deficiencies in the taxpayer’s claim. These deficiencies not only triggered the Department of Justice’s erroneous refund lawsuit and caused a total loss at the six-day bench trial, but also established the precise battlegrounds upon which the IRS and federal courts have subsequently invalidated R&D tax credit claims across the United States.
Failure to Contemporaneously Define Technological Uncertainty and Business Components

Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component.

At the district court level, the trial judge erroneously required McFerrin to prove that KMCO and KMTEX’s projects expanded or refined existing scientific principles in the chemical engineering field, met a "high threshold of innovation," and had a "broad effect". While the Fifth Circuit held that the district court erred by applying this heightened discovery standard instead of the regulatory "uncertainty" standard (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(ii)), it did not itself decide whether KMCO’s and KMTEX’s projects qualified; the district court had found that only a "few" projects "may have involved some research," and the government argued that most of the taxpayers’ activities did not constitute research at all, leaving for remand the distinction between routine chemical manufacturing adjustments and true design or method uncertainty.

In specialty and toll chemical manufacturing, engineers routinely adjust reaction temperatures, catalyst feed rates, distillation reflux ratios, and batch cycle times to meet customer purity specifications or adapt existing processes to available reactor vessels. The Fifth Circuit’s opinion does not describe the individual 1999 projects and makes no finding that KMCO’s and KMTEX’s retrospective study lumped together routine commercial production runs, quality control troubleshooting, and post-production debugging—which are explicitly excluded from qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(D)—with genuine process development; it records only the district court’s findings that there were no records of the hours worked on any given project, or of the hours worked or supplies used that involved research. When a taxpayer fails to isolate the specific business component (such as a discrete reaction synthesis pathway or distillation column configuration) and fails to record ex ante why known chemical engineering calculations could not establish the appropriate process design, trial courts inevitably view the activity as routine engineering rather than research aimed at eliminating technological uncertainty.
Absence of a Structured Process of Experimentation vs. Unstructured Trial and Error

To satisfy I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all of the research activities with respect to a business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. In the 2003 Final Regulations (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)), the Treasury defined a process of experimentation as a structured three-step methodology requiring first, the identification of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component; second, the identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and third, the identification and conduct of a process of evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology.

As noted in Footnote 5 of the Fifth Circuit’s opinion, the 2001 Proposed Regulations (which were in effect when McFerrin filed his amended returns in 2003) did not contain the three-step "process of experimentation" test of the 2003 Final Regulations and instead required a "facts and circumstances" test, and the government conceded at oral argument that McFerrin could rely on the definitions from the 2003 Regulations in defending the suit. The district court had relied on Eustace (312 F.3d at 907) and Norwest to hold that experimentation required formal scientific hypothesis formulation and testing, completely disqualifying engineering "trial and error".

Although the Fifth Circuit corrected the district court by affirming that systematic trial and error is a valid experimental evaluation method under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), this legal clarification highlights a critical evidentiary distinction—one the Fifth Circuit did not itself apply to KMCO’s and KMTEX’s projects but left for the district court on remand: the difference between systematic trial and error and haphazard or ad hoc trial and error. In chemical plant operations, simply changing a parameter when a batch fails specification—without a structured protocol identifying competing technical alternatives, holding confounding variables constant, and systematically evaluating the causal relationship between the altered parameter and the reaction outcome—does not satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i). Furthermore, under the "substantially all" rule of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), at least 80 percent of a business component's research activities (measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) must constitute elements of this structured process of experimentation. The opinion makes no finding that KMCO and KMTEX lacked experimental test plans, pilot-plant comparison logs, or failure-analysis records; it remanded so that the district court could apply the correct definitions and determine whether their plant-floor adjustments constituted a systematic evaluation of alternatives rather than routine operational tweaking.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Over-Reliance on Post-Hoc Oral Estimates

The government’s erroneous refund lawsuit was premised on a failure to substantiate: its complaint alleged that the amended return included no supporting documents, and the district court found no records substantiating the hours worked or supplies used that involved research in 1999. Under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a), every taxpayer is required to keep permanent books of account or records sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown on a tax return. Specifically, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) mandates that a taxpayer claiming a credit under I.R.C. § 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit". Although the preamble to T.D. 9104 noted that the 2001 Proposed Regulations and 2003 Final Regulations do not impose a specific rigid recordkeeping system beyond the general requirements of I.R.C. § 6001, the taxpayer must nonetheless produce reliable evidentiary proof linking claimed expenditures to qualified activities.

The district court determined that there were no records of the hours worked on any given project or of the hours worked or supplies used that involved research. Following the study KMCO commissioned from alliantgroup in May 2003, the claim rested on rough estimates given by employees years after the fact, which the district court was unwilling to credit; the opinion does not describe the consultants’ interview methodology.

While the Fifth Circuit rejected the government’s argument that the lack of documentation alone defeated the credit, holding that the district court should apply the Cohan rule (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540, 544 (2d Cir. 1930)) to estimate allowable QREs once qualified research activities are shown to have occurred, the appellate panel issued a sharp warning regarding McFerrin’s documentation failure. The Fifth Circuit reiterated the bedrock principle from Stinson Estate v. United States, 214 F.3d 846 (7th Cir. 2000), that tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, are only allowed as clearly provided for by statute, and are narrowly construed. Consequently, when a court makes an approximation under Cohan, it is expressly authorized to "bear heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making". Crucially, the Fifth Circuit held that "the district court need not credit McFerrin’s reconstruction of expenses from years after the fact" (citing Eustace v. Commissioner, 81 T.C.M. (CCH) 1370, *5 (2001)), instructing instead that the trial court should look to credible witness testimony, institutional knowledge of employees, and corroborating evidence in the record to determine a fair estimate.

The broader legal implications of this evidentiary deficiency became unmistakable in subsequent Fifth Circuit and Seventh Circuit decisions interpreting McFerrin. In Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, aff'd in part, vacated in part, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014)—a case involving another outside consultant’s R&D credit study—the taxpayers cited McFerrin to argue that the Tax Court was legally required to estimate R&D wage allocations under Cohan. The Tax Court rejected this contention, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed in part and vacated in part, with the reasoning indicating that McFerrin only triggers a Cohan estimate if the taxpayer first establishes a credible evidentiary baseline (citing Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559, 560 (5th Cir. 1957)) proving that the specific employees performed qualified services and providing a rational, non-speculative factual basis upon which to base an estimate. Similarly, in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the Seventh Circuit cited McFerrin for the availability of Cohan estimation, but affirmed complete disallowance of the credit because the taxpayer relied on arbitrary, unprincipled employee time estimates that could not prove the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). Thus, McFerrin and its progeny demonstrate that relying on retrospective oral percentages without objective documentary anchors exposes the taxpayer either to total disallowance for lack of a reasonable basis or a punitive Cohan reduction on remand.
Executive Compensation, Direct Supervision, and the I.R.C. § 174(e) Reasonableness Limitation

The most glaring financial vulnerability in McFerrin’s 1999 R&D credit claim was the inclusion of a $6.4 million bonus paid by KMCO to McFerrin in 1999 as a qualified wage expense. In Subchapter S corporations, shareholder-executives frequently extract corporate earnings through year-end bonuses rather than dividend distributions to manage tax and cash-flow objectives. The opinion does not state what portion of McFerrin’s $6.4 million bonus the amended return treated as a qualified research expense; the government contended that the bonus was not attributable to McFerrin’s research work and was not a "qualified research expense".

This strategy implicated three distinct statutory and regulatory barriers, the first and third of which were examined in McFerrin. The first barrier involves the distinction between compensation for "qualified services" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and a disguised return on equity. Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), "in-house research expenses" include "any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee". While I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) cross-references I.R.C. § 3401(a), and Treas. Reg. § 31.3401(a)-1 provides that wages include salaries, fees, and bonuses even when paid as a "percentage of profits", the district court determined only that McFerrin’s $6.4 million bonus was calculated based on the "profits and cash flow of KMCO in 1999" and not on the research performed that year, and made no findings on whether any portion constituted wages for qualified services that were reasonable under the circumstances.

The second barrier is the first-line "direct supervision" restriction codified in I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2). Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), qualified services consist strictly of engaging in qualified research, directly supervising qualified research, or directly supporting qualified research. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) defines "direct supervision" as the immediate, first-line management of qualified research, explicitly stipulating that "direct supervision does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". Although McFerrin was a prominent chemical engineer, as the co-founder of KMCO and owner of all of the related corporations, any managerial oversight by him of plant managers, lab directors, and commercial operations would constitute excluded upper-level management (an issue the Fifth Circuit did not address) unless he could prove specific hours spent personally conducting bench or plant experiments or acting as the immediate first-line supervisor of the experimenting engineers.

The third barrier is the statutory reasonableness limitation of I.R.C. § 174(e). Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), QREs must qualify as deductible research or experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174. Pursuant to I.R.C. § 174(e), research expenditures are deductible under § 174 only to the extent that the amount thereof is reasonable under the circumstances. In remanding the bonus issue, the Fifth Circuit declined to usurp the district court’s fact-finding role and left it to that court to determine under I.R.C. §§ 41(b) and 174(e) whether any portion of the $6.4 million bonus was part of McFerrin’s wages for qualified services he performed at KMCO and was "reasonable under the circumstances," as opposed to compensating him for his executive leadership and ownership of a profitable petrochemical enterprise.
Statutory Timing and Procedural Pleading Missteps

Finally, the McFerrin litigation highlighted two significant procedural failures. First, on summary judgment prior to the bench trial, McFerrin lost the entire R&D tax credit claim attributable to South Coast Terminals because SC Terminals’ amended 1999 return was filed outside the statutory limitations period under I.R.C. § 6511. In complex multi-entity pass-through structures involving tiered Subchapter S corporations and partnerships (where SC Acquisition and SC Delaware were partners in SC Terminals), failing to track entity-level return filing dates and extensions prior to executing a look-back study results in immediate statutory forfeiture of the refund claim.

Second, McFerrin’s first argument on appeal was that the substantiation claims should have been dismissed—challenging the government’s erroneous refund complaint under Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b) by seizing on phrasing in the complaint that McFerrin had "misrepresented facts" on his amended returns. The Fifth Circuit swiftly rejected this argument, clarifying that when the United States sues under I.R.C. § 7405 based on a taxpayer’s failure to substantiate claimed tax credits with adequate documentation, the claim sounds in statutory non-compliance rather than common-law fraud or mistake, rendering general notice pleading under Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2) fully sufficient.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement addressed in United States v. McFerrin against the taxpayer's operational or evidentiary failure, the district court's ruling, and the Fifth Circuit's controlling standard of proof.

cells: Erroneous Refund Recovery & Pleading Standard
Filed amended 1999 returns with no attached substantiating documentation; sought dismissal of DOJ complaint under Rule 9(b) particularity.
Denied Rule 9(b) motion to dismiss; tried the case under Rule 8(a)(2) notice pleading; held government met preponderance burden.

Affirmed on pleading: Lack of substantiation is not "fraud or mistake" under Rule 9(b); Rule 8(a)(2) governs. Under § 7405, the U.S. bears the ultimate burden of proving an erroneous refund occurred and its exact amount (Soltermann).
Timeliness of Pass-Through Refund Claims
Filed South Coast Terminals' amended 1999 return in September 2003 after the statutory limitations period had expired.
Granted partial summary judgment to the United States, ordering repayment of the refund portion relating to SC Terminals and its owners, SC Delaware and SC Acquisition.
Uncontested on appeal: Strict statutory filing deadlines apply to pass-through entity refund claims; untimely claims are barred as a matter of law.
Discovering Technological Information (Uncertainty Test)
The opinion identifies no specific documentation failure on this point; the district court found that only a few projects "may have involved some research".
Applied superseded case law (Tax & Accounting Software, Eustace, Norwest) requiring research to expand industry knowledge, meet a high threshold of innovation, and have a broad effect.

Vacated & Remanded: Taxpayers may rely on the 2001 Proposed and 2003 Final Regulations for prior years per T.D. 9104. "Discovering information" requires only intent to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or design of a business component.
Process of Experimentation Test
The opinion makes no finding on how the taxpayer’s experimentation was structured; the district court rejected "trial and error" testing as a matter of law.
Held that a "process of experimentation" requires formal scientific hypothesis formulation and testing, explicitly excluding engineering "trial and error" (Eustace).

Vacated & Remanded: Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation requires a 3-step process: (1) identify uncertainty, (2) identify alternatives, and (3) evaluate alternatives via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.
Substantiation & Judicial Estimation of QREs
I.R.C. § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d); Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)
Had no records of the hours worked on any given project or of the hours worked or supplies used that involved research; relied on rough estimates given by employees years after the fact.
Was unwilling to credit rough estimates given by employees years after the fact; did not estimate allowable expenses under the Cohan rule because it found no qualified research occurred.

Vacated & Remanded: While the court need not credit post-hoc reconstructions (Eustace), if qualified research activities are shown, the court should estimate allowable QREs under Cohan using testimony and institutional knowledge, and may bear heavily, if it chooses, on the taxpayer for inexactitude of its own making.
Executive Bonus & Qualified Services Allocation
Included a $6.4 million 1999 bonus paid to co-founder McFerrin in QREs; the district court found the bonus was calculated on KMCO’s 1999 profits and cash flow, not on research performed that year.

Found the $6.4 million bonus was determined based on KMCO's corporate profits and cash flow rather than research work performed in 1999, but made no findings on whether any portion was wages for qualified services that were reasonable under the circumstances.

Remanded for Factual Findings: Wages under § 3401(a) can include profit-percentage bonuses, but the trial court must determine under §§ 41(b) and 174(e) what portion represents reasonable compensation for qualified services actually performed by McFerrin.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate holdings of United States v. McFerrin—and the subsequent judicial guardrails established in Shami v. Commissioner, Trinity Industries v. United States, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner—into actionable compliance architecture, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how U.S. taxpayers can remediate the exact technical, contractual, compensation, and documentation failures exposed in the ruling.
Case Study 1: Specialty Petrochemical and Toll Manufacturing Scale-Up
Operational Scenario and Identified McFerrin Pitfalls

ChemSynth Holdings, Inc. ("ChemSynth") is a Texas-based Subchapter S corporation specializing in custom toll manufacturing and specialty chemical synthesis for the Gulf Coast petrochemical sector, broadly resembling KMCO’s manufacture of commodity and specialty chemicals for the petrochemical industry. During the current tax year, ChemSynth undertook "Project Alkylate-X," an initiative to scale up a high-purity polyalphaolefin (PAO) synthetic lubricant additive from a 5-liter laboratory glass reactor to a 10,000-gallon continuous-stirred tank reactor (CSTR) paired with a multi-stage fractional distillation column.

ChemSynth’s current tax posture exhibits four critical McFerrin vulnerabilities. First, during commercial scale-up, batches suffered from exothermic runaway risks and isomerization side-reactions, prompting plant engineers to adjust Friedel-Crafts catalyst dosing rates and distillation reboiler temperatures across 18 production runs without written test protocols; this creates an acute risk that an IRS examining engineer will classify the runs as routine commercial production and quality control under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and (D) rather than a structured process of experimentation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i). Second, ChemSynth’s founder and CEO, Dr. Vance (a Ph.D. chemical engineer owning 100 percent of the Subchapter S corporation), received a base salary of $350,000 and a year-end bonus of $4.8 million tied to corporate EBITDA; a third-party consultant proposed claiming 50 percent of Dr. Vance’s total compensation ( ($2,575,000) as QREs based on an oral interview stating he "oversaw all plant engineering," directly inviting challenge under I.R.C. § 174(e), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), and McFerrin / Shami. Third, ChemSynth’s 24 process engineers and lab technicians do not track time by project, booking all labor to a single plant overhead cost center and forcing reliance on retrospective oral percentage estimates. Fourth, raw petrochemical feedstocks used in experimental scale-up batches are billed to the general commercial inventory ledger, obscuring which supplies qualify under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).
Step 1: Project Governance and Business Component Segregation

To prevent routine commercial production from contaminating the R&D claim and causing Project Alkylate-X to fail the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), ChemSynth must restructure its internal project governance around the Business Component and Shrinking-Back rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Rather than defining the business component broadly as "PAO Manufacturing," ChemSynth’s R&D Governance Committee must charter Project Alkylate-X as a distinct process business component under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) and pre-emptively subdivide the project into three discrete sub-process components: Sub-Process 101 (Catalyst Injection and Exothermic Heat Transfer Control), Sub-Process 102 (Continuous Oligomerization Residence Time Distribution), and Sub-Process 103 (Vacuum Fractional Distillation Stripping). If the overall scale-up fails the 80 percent process-of-experimentation test due to commercial production runs, this sub-component architecture allows ChemSynth to legally invoke the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to preserve QREs for the specific sub-processes that independently satisfy the Four-Part Test. Furthermore, governance protocols must establish a hard "Commercial Release Gate" to comply with the post-production exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A). Once the CSTR operating parameters achieve target isomer purity (99.4 percent) and thermal stability across three consecutive validation batches, the R&D project code is locked, and all subsequent reactor runs are automatically routed to commercial cost-of-goods-sold (COGS) accounts.
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Uncertainty and Three-Step Experimentation

To satisfy the Fifth Circuit’s interpretation of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3) and (a)(5)(i) in McFerrin, ChemSynth must replace informal plant adjustments with a standardized Technical Uncertainty and Systematic Trial-and-Error Dossier. Prior to the first CSTR trial, the Lead Process Engineer must execute a Project Initiation Memo documenting under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) why existing literature, kinetic models, and 5-liter bench data cannot establish the appropriate design or method for the 10,000-gallon vessel, specifically detailing how the non-linear reduction in surface-area-to-volume ratio from bench to commercial scale creates heat-transfer and micromixing uncertainties that standard Reynolds number scaling correlations cannot resolve.

For each of the 18 scale-up runs, engineers must log data into a digital Batch Experimentation Matrix that maps directly to the three regulatory elements mandated by McFerrin under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i). The matrix must first state the specific uncertainty targeted (for example, the inability to prevent localized thermal hotspots exceeding 145°C during boron trifluoride co-catalyst addition), then identify the competing technical alternatives conceptualized to eliminate that uncertainty (such as multi-port subsurface sparger ring injection versus a pre-mixed static inline mixer feed upstream of the CSTR versus pulsed stoichiometric dosing with chilled heptane diluent), and finally record the systematic evaluation and analytical results. By documenting the chemometric simulation outputs, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) isomer profiles, and exothermic temperature curves for each run—explicitly recording why one alternative failed due to nozzle fouling and how another alternative was systematically modified across Runs 7 through 12 to eliminate the uncertainty—ChemSynth transforms informal plant tweaking into an audit-proof process of experimentation.
Step 3: Executive Compensation Restructuring and I.R.C. § 174(e) Compliance

To insulate Dr. Vance’s compensation from the government’s clawback challenge in McFerrin and the complete disallowance in Shami, ChemSynth must overhaul its corporate compensation agreements and supervisory documentation prior to the close of the taxable year. ChemSynth’s Board of Directors must adopt a formal Corporate Resolution and amended Executive Employment Agreement bifurcating Dr. Vance’s compensation into three distinct streams: a Base Salary of $350,000 compensating general executive and technical director duties; a Technical Milestone Incentive Bonus capped at $250,000 that is explicitly contingent upon Dr. Vance’s personal engineering execution and first-line supervision of chartered R&D scale-up projects (measured by patent filings, resolution of scale-up design uncertainties, and completion of pilot validation gates, rather than corporate EBITDA or cash flow); and a Shareholder S-Corporation Profit-Sharing Distribution of $4,550,000 explicitly designated as non-qualified return on equity that is completely excluded from the I.R.C. § 41 QRE calculation.

Concurrently, ChemSynth must retain an independent compensation valuation study benchmarking the total cash compensation of Chief Technology Officers and Principal Chemical Engineers in comparable Gulf Coast specialty chemical firms (establishing a reasonable market range of $400,000 to $600,000 annually). By capping Dr. Vance’s maximum eligible wage pool at $600,000 (comprising his Base Salary plus Technical Milestone Bonus) and applying his substantiated R&D time percentage solely to that reasonable compensation pool, ChemSynth satisfies I.R.C. § 174(e) and eliminates the distortion of applying R&D percentages to a multi-million-dollar profit bonus. Furthermore, to overcome the upper-level manager exclusion of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), Dr. Vance must not claim time spent supervising the Vice President of Manufacturing or Plant Manager. Instead, the organizational chart for Project Alkylate-X must designate Dr. Vance as the direct, first-line Project Leader to whom the experimenting process engineers report directly for technical sign-off, and Dr. Vance must personally sign and annotate the weekly Batch Experimentation Matrices to create contemporaneous documentary proof of engaging in and directly supervising qualified research.
Step 4: Experimentation Cost and Time Tracking to Fortify the Cohan Baseline

To satisfy I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)—and ensure that if judicial estimation is ever required, the taxpayer possesses an unassailable evidentiary foundation under McFerrin and Williams—ChemSynth must configure its Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system with specific work-order codes for Sub-Processes 101, 102, and 103. Process engineers and lab technicians must complete bi-weekly electronic timecards allocating hours across R&D sub-process codes and non-qualified commercial operations, approved by their immediate supervisor. Raw chemical feedstocks drawn for experimental trial batches must be requisitioned using a dedicated R&D Material Issue Code tied to the specific sub-process work order, segregating qualified supplies under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) from commercial inventory. Where exact hourly logs are incomplete for salaried chemical engineers, ChemSynth must compile contemporaneous objective metadata—including Distributed Control System (DCS) operator login timestamps during experimental batch runs, laboratory notebook sign-offs, Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) sample test timestamps, and engineering change order (ECO) authorship logs. Under McFerrin, presenting a trial court or IRS examiner with timestamped DCS batch logs and LIMS test records anchored to specific engineers provides the concrete institutional evidence necessary to compel a favorable Cohan estimate without suffering a punitive judicial reduction.

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Process Equipment and Custom Vessel Fabrication
Operational Scenario and Identified McFerrin Pitfalls

Apex Process Systems LLC ("Apex"), an Indiana-based corporation taxed under Subchapter S, designs and fabricates custom modular chemical processing skids and high-pressure reactor vessels for industrial clients—an operational setting directly implicating the doctrinal intersection of United States v. McFerrin, Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014), and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023).

Apex entered into a contract with a commercial chemical producer ("Client") to design and build a first-of-its-kind Supercritical Extraction Vessel Skid ("Skid-7"). Because Apex had never built a supercritical extraction system operating at 5,000 psi with corrosive co-solvents, its mechanical and chemical engineers performed Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling to design the custom pressure vessel closure mechanism and internal acoustic cavitation nozzles, while using standard off-the-shelf ASME code calculations to fabricate the structural steel frame, piping manifolds, and electrical control panels.

Apex’s claim faces four severe legal pitfalls identified in McFerrin and its appellate progeny. First, Apex claimed the entire Skid-7 fabrication cost ($4.2 million in wages and supplies) as a single business component on the theory that the skid was "new to Apex"; because 65 percent of the total labor hours on Skid-7 involved routine ASME welding, structural frame assembly, and standard piping layout—which do not involve a process of experimentation—the entire Skid-7 project fails the 80 percent "substantially all" numerator/denominator test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Second, Apex did not segregate engineering design hours from shop-floor fabrication and testing hours, relying instead on management's arbitrary estimate that 85 percent of all engineering and shop labor was experimental—a methodology rejected in Little Sandy Coal and McFerrin. Third, Apex’s contract with Client provides for progress payments and contains ambiguous warranty and acceptance clauses, raising an immediate IRS challenge that the research is excluded as "funded research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). Fourth, when weld cracks appeared during hydrostatic testing of the vessel nozzle, Apex paid a third-party lab to X-ray the welds and claimed the cost as contract research, despite lacking any experimental protocol, an expenditure vulnerable to classification as routine quality-control testing, consistent with the substantiation failures in Little Sandy Coal.
Step 1: Project Governance and Sub-Component "Shrinking-Back" Architecture

To prevent the non-experimental fabrication of standard skid components from disqualifying the entire Skid-7 project under the 80 percent "substantially all" rule of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), Apex must restructure its work breakdown structure (WBS) at project inception. Instead of treating the entire Skid-7 unit as a single monolithic business component, Apex’s engineering governance must decompose Skid-7 into discrete, functionally independent sub-components in its WBS and computer-aided design (CAD) bill of materials (BOM): Sub-Component A (WBS-701: High-Pressure Quick-Actuating Breach-Lock Closure Assembly), Sub-Component B (WBS-702: Supercritical Co-Solvent Ultrasonic Cavitation Mixing Nozzle), and Sub-Component C (WBS-703: Structural Steel Skid Frame, Standard ASME Piping Manifolds, and PLC Control Cabinet). By isolating WBS-701 and WBS-702 as separate business components under the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and completely excluding WBS-703 from the R&D tax credit claim, Apex removes all routine structural welding and standard piping hours from the denominator of the "substantially all" fraction. Within WBS-701 and WBS-702, over 90 percent of the engineering, FEA/CFD simulation, and prototype machining hours constitute elements of a process of experimentation, easily surpassing the 80 percent statutory threshold.
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Design Uncertainty and Iterative Modeling Logs

To establish under McFerrin that WBS-701 and WBS-702 were undertaken to "discover information" by eliminating capability or design uncertainty rather than merely applying known engineering calculations, Apex must implement a rigorous engineering documentation protocol. In Little Sandy Coal, the Seventh Circuit emphasized that merely using engineering calculations and modeling to design a first-time vessel does not automatically constitute a process of experimentation if the engineers knew at the outset that standard calculations would achieve the design goal. Therefore, Apex’s Lead Mechanical Engineer must author a Design Uncertainty Brief for WBS-701 and WBS-702 proving why standard ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC) Section VIII Division 1 formulas could not establish an appropriate seal geometry or nozzle configuration under rapid supercritical decompression cycles, specifically documenting explosive decompression elastomer failure and non-linear thermal stress gradients.

Apex must then maintain a version-controlled Iterative Evaluation Ledger linking every CAD revision (Rev 1.0 through Rev 6.4) of the breach-lock closure and cavitation nozzle to specific FEA and CFD simulation runs. Each ledger entry must record the specific geometric or metallurgical alternative evaluated (such as Inconel 718 versus Nitronic 60 sealing rings, or 15-degree versus 22-degree converging nozzle angles), the simulated stress-intensity or cavitation-index output, the physical hydrostatic or flow-loop prototype test results, and the technical rationale explaining why the iteration succeeded or failed. Furthermore, to reduce the substantiation risk illustrated by Little Sandy Coal, routine non-destructive examination (NDE) X-ray testing of standard production welds to verify ASME code compliance must be booked to WBS-703 as non-qualified quality control under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(D). Conversely, destructive metallurgical testing and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) performed to evaluate experimental laser-cladding alternatives on the WBS-702 cavitation nozzle must be contracted under a specific Test Protocol Memo tied directly to WBS-702’s design uncertainty.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring to Defeat the Funded Research Exclusion

Even if Apex satisfies all four prongs of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) under McFerrin, its credit claim will be disqualified under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) if the research is "funded" by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), to prevent research performed under a customer contract from being excluded as funded research, the taxpayer must both bear the financial risk of failure (meaning payment is contingent on the technical success of the research) and retain substantial rights in the research results.

To satisfy the financial risk prong, Apex must replace time-and-materials or unconditional progress billing in its Master Engineering and Fabrication Agreement with a firm fixed-price structure where all milestone advances are legally refundable if Skid-7 fails to achieve the specified supercritical extraction performance metrics during Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT). Specifically, the contract must stipulate that payment of the contract price is strictly contingent upon Apex successfully designing and delivering a system that meets the quantitative performance guarantees, and that if Apex fails to overcome the technical design uncertainties to achieve those guarantees, the client may reject the system, receive a full refund of all prior milestone payments, and leave Apex bearing 100 percent of all engineering, material, and rework costs. To satisfy the substantial rights prong, the contract’s intellectual property clause must explicitly vest in Apex unrestricted ownership and usage rights to all foreground process engineering, sub-component designs (specifically WBS-701 and WBS-702 architectures), and technical know-how developed during the contract, granting Apex the right to utilize such designs and discoveries in the manufacture of equipment for other commercial customers without paying royalties or fees to the client.
Step 4: Granular Experimentation Tracking to Satisfy the "Substantially All" Numerator and Cohan Standard

To ensure that Apex can mathematically prove the 80 percent "substantially all" fraction under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and satisfy the substantiation mandates of McFerrin and Little Sandy Coal, Apex must require all engineers, CAD designers, and prototype machinists to log time daily against both a Sub-Component Code (WBS-701, WBS-702, WBS-703) and a four-tier Activity Phase Code. Under this structure, Code E-1 captures uncertainty identification and alternative conceptualization under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i); Code E-2 captures iterative CAD modeling, FEA/CFD simulation, and systematic prototype fabrication and testing; Code R-1 captures post-uncertainty final production shop drawings and routine tolerance checks on WBS-701 and WBS-702 (which constitute non-experimental research or engineering activities included in the denominator under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)); and Code C-1 captures all routine commercial fabrication, assembly, and ASME code testing on WBS-703.

By maintaining contemporaneous daily time logs segregated by sub-component and experimental activity phase, supported by CAD and FEA file-save timestamps and prototype shop traveler sign-offs, Apex eliminates any reliance on post-hoc oral estimates. Should an IRS examination or judicial proceeding ever challenge a subset of hours, Apex possesses the exact, principled evidentiary foundation required by the Fifth Circuit in United States v. McFerrin to compel allowance of the credit.
Conclusion and Strategic Practice Takeaways

United States v. McFerrin remains a foundational pillar of U.S. R&D tax credit jurisprudence because it simultaneously rescued taxpayers from an impossibly high judicial standard of scientific discovery while exposing the fatal evidentiary flaws of retrospective, interview-based tax credit studies. On the doctrinal side, the Fifth Circuit cemented the principle that qualifying research under I.R.C. § 41 does not require pioneering breakthroughs that expand the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor does it require formal laboratory hypothesis testing; rather, activities aimed at eliminating capability, method, or design uncertainty regarding a business component through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error fully satisfy the statute under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4. Furthermore, the Fifth Circuit confirmed that the Cohan rule applies to I.R.C. § 41, directing that trial courts should estimate allowable QREs when a taxpayer proves that qualified research activities occurred.

However, practitioners and corporate tax directors must read McFerrin alongside its subsequent judicial interpretation in Shami v. Commissioner, Trinity Industries v. United States, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner. Those decisions demonstrate that McFerrin’s endorsement of the Cohan rule is not a license to dispense with contemporaneous recordkeeping under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d). Trial courts are under no obligation to credit post-hoc oral time reconstructions fabricated years after the tax year, and they will refuse to apply Cohan altogether if the taxpayer fails to establish a rational, non-speculative evidentiary foundation proving both the performance of qualified services and compliance with the 80 percent "substantially all" process-of-experimentation threshold. By proactively structuring R&D projects into granular sub-components under the shrinking-back rule, documenting baseline uncertainties and three-step experimental evaluations in real time, insulating executive compensation from profit-sharing distortions under I.R.C. § 174(e) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), and capturing objective time and metadata logs, U.S. taxpayers can satisfy the strict scrutiny of the IRS and federal courts.
